sentences.text: The fossil preserves body remains, primary and secondary feathers, and a bastard wing covered in limonite. Eoalulavis was roughly the size of a European goldfinch, with bony wing elements measuring about 17 centimeters. Upon discovery, it was noted to be the size of a modern goldfinch with a wingspan of about 17 centimeters.

Some researchers describe the unique shape of the Eoalulavis sternum as "spear-shaped" or "fish-shaped". The forelimb morphology includes large ungual phalanges on the alular and major digits, with the minor digit bearing two phalanges.

At the time of its discovery, Eoalulavis was the earliest known bird to possess an alula, a structure used for flight stability. This fossil provided the first direct evidence of feeding behavior in Enantiornithes and Mesozoic birds.

Later studies estimated the bird weighed approximately 45 grams with a total wingspan of about 26 centimeters. This fossil provided the first direct evidence of feeding behavior in Enantiornithes and Mesozoic birds.
The genus Eoalulavis was named by Sanz and colleagues in 1996. Fossils of Eoalulavis were found at the Las Hoyas Konservat-Lagerstätte in Cuenca, Spain.
Research indicates Eoalulavis could perform continuous flapping flight but was likely unable to glide due to its body mass.

The holotype preserves crustacean cuticles in the abdomen area, interpreted as the bird's last meal. Researchers interpret the diet evidence as suggesting Eoalulavis lived in shorelines seeking invertebrates like modern turnstones. The holotype shows crustacean exoskeleton remains in the thoracic cavity, interpreted as fossilized stomach contents.
Eoalulavis is believed to have been the most adapted to a semi-aquatic environment among the local avifauna.

Recent cladistic analyses group Eoalulavis with the genus Liaoningornis as a derived group of Enantiornithes. Eoalulavis is classified within Enantiornithes based on traits like a groove in the radius or a foramen in the coracoids.

Eoalulavis lived during the Barremian stage of the Lower Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago. The Las Hoyas locality was a seasonal subtropical wetland dominated by aquatic organisms during the Barremian. The fossil record for Eoalulavis spans from 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago.
